passage:
"Hello, Pema. I'm Dr Arnab. Your mummy says your cough is noisy."
Pema pressed her face into Mummy's arm.
"Do you know what this is?" He held up the stethoscope.
"...A snake?"
"Ha! It's a listening tube. Want to hear your own heart first?"
He put the ends gently in her ears and the round part on her chest.
"It goes thump-thump!"
"That's you. Now can I listen too?"
Pema sat up and pulled up her top herself. "Listen to my thump-thump."
"Very strong," said Dr Arnab. Pema grinned.

qa.q: What did Pema first think the stethoscope was?
qa.a: She thought it was a snake.

qa.q: How did Pema's feelings change after she heard her heart?
qa.a: She went from afraid, pressing her face into Mummy's arm, to curious and brave, pulling up her top herself.

qa.q: What did Dr Arnab do that helped Pema trust him?
qa.a: He spoke kindly, explained the tool and let her listen to her own heart first, so she felt included.

qa.q: How might Mummy feel watching Pema sit up and grin?
qa.a: She probably feels relieved that the check-up became easy and her daughter was not frightened.

grounding: A doctor explains the stethoscope and lets a young child listen, so she feels less afraid, curious and trusting.

passage:
Note from Kiran's mum, Trisha, for his class teacher.
Kiran missed school yesterday for a check-up. In the waiting room he hid under my dupatta and said, "No doctor." When we went in, the doctor knelt down and said, "This is my ear tube. Want to try?" and let Kiran listen to her heart. He giggled, then asked to listen to mine. After that he held still and even opened his mouth wide for the torch. On the way home he said, "She let me be a doctor too." He may want to tell you about it!

qa.q: Where did Kiran hide in the waiting room?
qa.a: He hid under his mum's dupatta.

qa.q: How did Kiran feel after the doctor let him listen?
qa.a: He felt less afraid and curious, even giggling and asking to listen to his mum's heart.

qa.q: Why did the doctor's approach help Kiran trust her?
qa.a: Including him by letting him try the ear tube made him feel brave and part of what was happening.

qa.q: How might the doctor see Kiran's giggle?
qa.a: She may feel pleased that her small trick turned a scared child into a willing helper.

grounding: A doctor lets a young boy listen with the stethoscope, and his fear turns into curiosity and trust.

passage:
Monday: Francis had a fever. Mummy brought him jelly and let him lie on her bed with the cartoons on. Kishore stood in the doorway, arms folded.
Tuesday: Francis got orange juice with a straw. Kishore coughed loudly. "I think I'm sick too." Mummy felt his forehead. "Hmm, you're cool." Kishore stomped away. "Nobody brings ME jelly."
Wednesday: Mummy took Kishore to the balcony. "Francis needs rest to get better. But I miss you. This is our time." They shared a bowl of jelly and watered the plants. Kishore leaned on her.

qa.q: What did Francis get on Tuesday?
qa.a: Francis got orange juice with a straw.

qa.q: Why did Kishore cough loudly and say he was sick too?
qa.a: He felt jealous of the attention and treats Francis was getting, and wished he could be sick too.

qa.q: What did Mummy do on Wednesday that helped Kishore?
qa.a: She explained that Francis needed rest and gave Kishore special time on the balcony, sharing jelly and watering plants.

qa.q: How might Francis feel lying on Mummy's bed while Kishore stands in the doorway?
qa.a: He may feel too unwell to notice much, or a little awkward seeing his brother cross.

grounding: Over a few days, a young boy is jealous of his sick brother's attention and treats, and his mother explains and gives him care time too.

passage: Papa was away on work, and the lights kept going off. Mummy was alone with Madhav, who was hot with fever and whimpering. She sat with him all evening, pressing a wet cloth on his head and feeding him soup. Neelam sat on the floor, hugging her knees. "I want soup in bed too. I wish I was sick." Mummy looked up, tired. Then she patted the mattress. "Come. Madhav needs to rest so he gets better. But you can have soup here, next to me." Neelam curled beside her, and Mummy told her a story in the dark.

qa.q: Why was Mummy alone with the children?
qa.a: Papa was away on work.

qa.q: What was Neelam feeling when she said she wished she was sick?
qa.a: She felt jealous and left out, watching Mummy care for Madhav all evening.

qa.q: How did Mummy handle Neelam's jealousy even though she was tired?
qa.a: She explained that Madhav needed rest and still made space for Neelam beside her, with soup and a story.

qa.q: How might Mummy feel hearing Neelam say "I wish I was sick"?
qa.a: She may feel stretched and tired, but she understands it as a normal wish for care, not naughtiness.

grounding: A young girl feels jealous of her sick brother and wishes she were sick too, and her tired mother explains and includes her.

passage: Dolma had a sore throat and a hot forehead. She lay on the sofa in their Delhi flat, holding the end of Mummy's kurta. "Don't go." Mummy needed to fetch medicine from the chemist downstairs. Dolma started to cry. "Don't leave me!" Mummy knelt. "I'll be back when the big hand of the clock is on the six. Papa will sit with you." Papa, Yusuf, sat down and held Dolma's hand. Dolma watched the clock the whole time. When the door opened, she reached up with both arms. Mummy held her close. "See? I came back."

qa.q: Where did Mummy need to go?
qa.a: She needed to fetch medicine from the chemist downstairs.

qa.q: Why did Dolma hold the end of Mummy's kurta?
qa.a: She felt afraid and helpless while she was ill, and wanted Mummy close so she would feel safe.

qa.q: What did Mummy do that helped Dolma's fear?
qa.a: She told Dolma exactly when she would be back, left her with Papa, and kept her promise.

qa.q: How might Yusuf feel sitting with Dolma while she watches the clock?
qa.a: He may feel tender and a little helpless, knowing she really wants her mother right now.

grounding: A sick young girl clings to her mother and is afraid when she leaves, and her mother says when she will be back and keeps her word.

passage:
"Mummy, where are you going?"
"Just to the kitchen, Parveen. To make your rice."
"No! Stay!"
Hafsa sat back down on the bed. Parveen's cheeks were flushed and her voice was croaky. She wrapped both arms around Hafsa's waist.
"You feel scared when you're sick, hmm?"
"Yes. Everything is too big."
"I'll stay till you're sleepy. Then I'll make rice and come back. Keep my scarf, so you know I'm coming."
Parveen held the scarf against her cheek.
"Promise?"
"Promise. I always come back."

qa.q: What did Hafsa leave with Parveen?
qa.a: She left her scarf with Parveen.

qa.q: What does Parveen wrapping her arms around Hafsa suggest?
qa.a: She felt scared and helpless while sick, as if everything was too big, and needed her mother close to feel safe.

qa.q: How did Hafsa treat Parveen's clinging?
qa.a: She saw it as a need for safety, not naughtiness, stayed close, and told her when she would come back.

qa.q: What would change if Hafsa had said "Stop being a baby"?
qa.a: Parveen might feel more frightened and ashamed, and cling even harder.

grounding: A sick young girl clings to her mother, who stays close, names her fear and tells her when she will return.

passage: In their garden in Aarhus, Emil found Mor sitting by Bamse's basket. The old dog wasn't moving. "Is Bamse sleeping?" Mor, Yara, pulled him onto her lap. "No, sweetheart. Bamse died this morning. His body stopped working. He can't wake up again." Emil cried and cried. "Where did he go? When will he come back?" "He won't come back. That's why we're so sad." Emil sobbed into her jumper until he was tired. Later he drew Bamse with a big red ball. "So he can play," he said, and they put the picture in the basket.

qa.q: What did Emil draw Bamse with?
qa.a: He drew Bamse with a big red ball.

qa.q: How was Emil feeling when he asked when Bamse would come back?
qa.a: He felt deep sadness and confusion, not yet understanding that Bamse was gone forever.

qa.q: What did Yara do that wise adults do when a pet dies?
qa.a: She told the truth in simple words, let Emil cry as long as he needed, and helped him say goodbye with a drawing.

qa.q: What is it like for Yara to tell Emil the news?
qa.a: She is sad too, but she holds him close and stays calm so he can grieve safely.

grounding: A young boy's dog dies, and his mother tells him the truth simply, lets him cry and helps him say goodbye with a drawing.

passage: At the animal clinic, Sachin waited on the bench, swinging his legs. Then Dr Madhav came out slowly and knelt in front of him and Papa. "Sachin, Tuffy was very old and very sick. He died a little while ago. His body stopped working." Sachin's face crumpled. "Can you fix him?" "No, I can't. When someone dies, they don't come back." Sachin cried against Papa's chest, big hiccupping sobs. Dr Madhav waited. Then he asked, "Would you like to say goodbye?" Sachin nodded and stroked Tuffy's ear, very gently. "Bye, Tuffy."

qa.q: What did Sachin stroke to say goodbye?
qa.a: He stroked Tuffy's ear, very gently.

qa.q: What does Sachin asking "Can you fix him?" show about his feelings?
qa.a: He felt sad and confused, not yet understanding that death is forever.

qa.q: Which choices by Dr Madhav were wise?
qa.a: He used simple, honest words, waited while Sachin cried and offered him a chance to say goodbye.

qa.q: How might Papa feel holding Sachin as he sobs?
qa.a: Papa probably feels sad too and protective, wishing he could take away his son's pain. 🤍

grounding: A young boy learns his old dog has died at the clinic, and the vet tells him the truth simply and lets him cry and say goodbye.

passage: It was Anand's birthday morning, and the relatives would arrive at noon. But Moti, their old dog, had died in the night. Anand sat by Moti's empty mat and cried. An aunty on the phone said, "Tell him to stop crying, it's his birthday! Get a new puppy." His mother, Devika, put down the phone. She sat on the floor and hugged him tight. "It is okay to be sad. We loved Moti very much." Anand sobbed. "Can I be sad on my birthday?" "You can. We'll cut the cake later, when you're ready." Anand leaned against her, still crying.

qa.q: When were the relatives going to arrive?
qa.a: The relatives would arrive at noon.

qa.q: How did Anand feel when Devika hugged him and said it was okay to be sad?
qa.a: He felt understood and allowed to grieve, even though it was his birthday and he was still very sad.

qa.q: Why was Devika's response wiser than the aunty's?
qa.a: She let Anand cry and named their love for Moti, instead of telling him to stop or offering a new puppy.

qa.q: What would change if Devika had followed the aunty's advice?
qa.a: Anand might hide his sadness and feel his love for Moti didn't matter.

grounding: On his birthday a young boy's old dog dies, and his mother hugs him and says it's okay to be sad instead of telling him to stop crying.

passage: Nilesh's goldfish, Bubbles, was floating at the top of the bowl in their Mumbai flat. Nilesh stared, then burst into tears. Dadi called from the kitchen, "Don't cry, we'll buy another one from the market." Nilesh cried harder. His papa, Kiran, came and sat on the floor. He wrapped Nilesh in a hug. "It is okay to be sad. We loved Bubbles very much." "He was my fish," Nilesh sobbed. "Yes. He was yours. Nobody can be Bubbles again." Nilesh cried until his shirt was wet. Then he asked, "Can we bury him in the plant pot?" Kiran nodded.

qa.q: What did Dadi suggest when Nilesh cried?
qa.a: She said they would buy another one from the market.

qa.q: How did Nilesh feel when Kiran said "Nobody can be Bubbles again"?
qa.a: He felt understood in his sadness, as if his love for Bubbles was taken seriously.

qa.q: What did Kiran do instead of offering a new fish?
qa.a: He hugged Nilesh, said it was okay to be sad and agreed to bury Bubbles in the plant pot.

qa.q: Why might Dadi react differently from Kiran?
qa.a: Dadi may want to stop Nilesh's pain quickly, so she offers a replacement instead of letting him grieve.

grounding: A young boy's goldfish dies, and his father hugs him and says it's okay to be sad instead of offering a new pet.

passage:
"Ammi, is Chintu dead because of me?"
Minakshi stopped folding clothes. "Why do you think that, Noor?"
"Yesterday I forgot to give him his seeds. And last week I was angry when he bit my finger. I said, 'Go away, bad bird.'"
Noor's chin shook. Minakshi pulled her close.
"Listen to me, jaan. Chintu died because he was very old. It was not because of anything you did or said."
"Not my angry words?"
"Not your angry words. Words can't make a bird die."
Noor cried into her lap, and Minakshi held her.

qa.q: What did Noor say when Chintu bit her finger?
qa.a: She said, "Go away, bad bird."

qa.q: Why did Noor think Chintu died because of her?
qa.a: She felt guilty, believing that forgetting his seeds and her angry words could have caused his death.

qa.q: What did Minakshi say that helped Noor?
qa.a: She said clearly that Chintu died because he was very old, not because of anything Noor did or said.

qa.q: How might Minakshi feel when Noor asks if it was her fault?
qa.a: She probably feels sad and tender, wanting to lift that heavy guilt off her daughter.

grounding: A young girl believes her forgotten feeding and angry words caused her bird's death, and her mother clearly tells her it was not her fault.

passage:
Note from Chinmay Sir, class teacher, to Bhupen's parents.
Today Bhupen was very quiet. At story time he whispered to me, "Our cat Billu died because I shouted at him. I told him I didn't like him anymore." He looked very scared. I knelt down and said, "Bhupen, Billu did not die because of anything you did or said. Shouting can't make a cat die." He asked me twice more, and I said the same each time. Then he drew Billu sleeping in the sun. Please tell him the same at home. He needs to hear it from you too.

qa.q: What did Bhupen draw?
qa.a: He drew Billu sleeping in the sun.

qa.q: What was Bhupen afraid of when he whispered to Chinmay Sir?
qa.a: He felt guilty and scared that his shouting had made Billu die.

qa.q: Why did Chinmay Sir repeat the same answer each time?
qa.a: Young children believe their thoughts can cause things, so hearing a clear "not your fault" again and again helps it sink in.

qa.q: How might Bhupen's parents feel reading this note?
qa.a: They may feel sad that he has been carrying this guilt and want to reassure him at home.

grounding: A young boy believes his shouting caused his cat to die, and his teacher clearly and repeatedly tells him it was not his fault.

passage: In the backyard in Sydney, Layla knelt by the lemon tree and cried for Pepper, their cat. Aiko stood beside her big sister. She didn't know what to say. Her own eyes started to sting. She sat down and put her arms around Layla. Layla held her back. They stayed like that for a long time. Then Mum came out with a small pot of yellow daisies. "Shall we plant these for Pepper?" The sisters dug the hole together with their hands. Aiko patted the soil flat. "Now we can visit her every day," she said.

qa.q: What did Mum bring out?
qa.a: Mum brought out a small pot of yellow daisies.

qa.q: How did Aiko feel watching Layla cry?
qa.a: She felt sad too, her own eyes stinging, and unsure what to say.

qa.q: How did planting the daisies help the sisters?
qa.a: It gave them a shared way to remember Pepper and a place to visit every day.

qa.q: What is it like for Layla when Aiko puts her arms around her?
qa.a: Layla probably feels comforted and less alone in her sadness. 🤍

grounding: A young girl feels sad watching her sister grieve their cat; they hold each other and plant a flower to remember.

passage: At the vet clinic, Charu sat on the plastic chair and cried for Guddu, their rabbit. Harish, her little brother, sat beside her. He watched her tears drop on her frock. His chest felt heavy. He took her hand. Charu pulled him into a hug, and they cried together. The vet nurse came with two cups of water and a small paper packet. "Marigold seeds. Some families plant a flower to remember." That evening, in the pot on their balcony, Charu made the holes and Harish dropped in the seeds. "For Guddu," he whispered.

qa.q: What was in the small paper packet?
qa.a: It held marigold seeds.

qa.q: What was Harish feeling as he watched Charu's tears?
qa.a: He felt sad and heavy in his chest, sharing his sister's sadness for Guddu.

qa.q: How did the vet nurse help the children?
qa.a: The nurse offered a small ritual, planting a flower, giving them a way to remember Guddu together.

qa.q: How might Charu feel when Harish takes her hand?
qa.a: She likely feels comforted and less alone, which is why she pulls him into a hug.

grounding: A young boy feels sad watching his sister cry for their rabbit; they hug and plant marigold seeds to remember him.

passage:
Note from Harish's class teacher.
Harish told the class his dog Sheru had died. Ojas said, "It's just a dog. Get another." Harish went still, then his face crumpled. He said, loudly, "He was my friend!" I was proud of him for saying that. I knelt beside Ojas and explained that Sheru was like family, and asked, "What could you say instead?" Ojas thought and said, "Sorry about Sheru." Harish nodded. Children often don't know what to say yet. We will practise gentle words this week.

qa.q: What did Ojas say about Sheru?
qa.a: Ojas said, "It's just a dog. Get another."

qa.q: How did Harish feel when Ojas said that?
qa.a: He felt hurt and misunderstood, his face crumpling, because Sheru was his friend.

qa.q: How did the teacher help Ojas learn gentle words?
qa.a: The teacher explained that Sheru was like family and asked Ojas what to say instead, and Ojas chose "Sorry about Sheru."

qa.q: Why might Ojas have said something so unkind?
qa.a: Ojas probably didn't know what to say about death and didn't mean to hurt Harish.

grounding: A young boy's friend calls his dead dog "just a dog"; he says "He was my friend", and a teacher teaches gentler words.

passage: By the village pond, Pradeep sat with his knees up. Their buffalo calf, Lali, had died. Binita came running with a stick. "Come and play! Why are you sad? It's just a calf. Your father will get another." Pradeep's throat got tight. He turned away. Binita poked him. "Come on!" Pradeep said, "Lali was my friend. I fed her every day." Binita stopped. Binita's grandmother, sitting on the steps, called out, "Binita, when your hen died, how did you feel?" Binita looked at her feet. Then she sat beside Pradeep. "Sorry about Lali."

qa.q: Which animal had died?
qa.a: Their buffalo calf, Lali, had died.

qa.q: How did Pradeep feel when Binita said "It's just a calf"?
qa.a: He felt hurt and misunderstood; his throat got tight and he turned away.

qa.q: What wise thing did Pradeep say?
qa.a: He told Binita, "Lali was my friend. I fed her every day," so she could understand his loss.

qa.q: How did Binita's grandmother help Binita see Pradeep's side?
qa.a: She asked Binita how she felt when her own hen died, which helped her feel what Pradeep was feeling and say sorry.

grounding: A young boy's friend dismisses the death of his calf, he explains she was his friend, and an adult helps the friend find gentle words.

passage: In the school library, Rukmini sat on the rug holding a book about a granny who tells stories. Her eyes filled. "My Nani died," she told her class teacher. "Where is she now? Will she come for my sports day?" The teacher sat beside her. "Nani died. Her body stopped working, so she can't come back. What does your family say about where she is?" "Amma says she is a star." "That's a lovely thought." Divyansh came over. "My Dada died too." Rukmini asked again, "Can she come for sports day?" The teacher answered gently again. "No, she can't. But you can tell me one of her stories."

qa.q: What was the library book about?
qa.a: It was about a granny who tells stories.

qa.q: Why did Rukmini ask her question again?
qa.a: She felt sad and confused about where Nani is and couldn't yet understand that she wouldn't come back.

qa.q: What did the teacher do that fits wise grief support?
qa.a: The teacher used simple, honest words, answered the same question again patiently and invited Rukmini to share one of Nani's stories.

qa.q: How might Divyansh feel hearing about Rukmini's Nani?
qa.a: Divyansh may feel sad and connected, remembering the Dada who died too.

grounding: A young girl misses her Nani and asks where she is again and again, and a teacher answers simply, honestly and patiently.

passage:
Monday: After Nani's funeral, Seema kept asking, "When will Nani come back?" Her big sister Avni said, "Nani died. She can't come back." Seema cried and hid under Nani's shawl.
Wednesday: At bedtime Seema asked again. "Where is Nani?" Mummy said again, softly, "She died. We can't see her anymore, but we can remember her." Seema missed Nani's lap and the crow story.
Sunday: Avni brought the photo album. They found Nani laughing at the beach. Avni told the crow story, the way Nani did. Seema giggled at the funny voice.

qa.q: What story did Seema miss?
qa.a: She missed Nani's crow story.

qa.q: What does Seema hiding under Nani's shawl suggest?
qa.a: She felt deep sadness and confusion, wanting to be close to Nani and not understanding why she can't come back.

qa.q: How did the family help Seema over the week?
qa.a: They used simple honest words each time she asked, then kept Nani's memory alive with photos and the crow story.

qa.q: How might Avni feel telling the crow story the way Nani did?
qa.a: She may feel sad and missing Nani herself, but warm that she can help her little sister remember.

grounding: Over a week, a young girl misses her Nani and keeps asking where she is, and her family answers honestly and keeps Nani's memory alive.

passage:
Note from Pankaj, Nitin's papa, for his class teacher.
My mother, Nitin's Dadi, died last week. On Sunday Nitin found me crying on the balcony. He stood very still and went quiet, then asked, "Papa, are you sick?" He looked scared. I pulled him onto my lap and said, "I am sad because I miss Dadi. It is okay to be sad. I am still here for you." He touched my wet cheek and said, "I miss her too." We cried together a little. He may be quiet at school. Please let me know if he seems worried.

qa.q: Where did Nitin find his papa crying?
qa.a: He found him crying on the balcony.

qa.q: What does Nitin asking "Papa, are you sick?" suggest he felt?
qa.a: He felt scared and worried, not understanding why his father was crying.

qa.q: What did Pankaj say that helped Nitin?
qa.a: He named his sadness about missing Dadi, said it is okay to be sad and told Nitin he was still there for him.

qa.q: How might Nitin's class teacher use this note?
qa.a: The teacher can be gentle with Nitin, notice if he seems quiet or worried, and tell his papa.

grounding: A young boy is scared to see his father crying for Dadi, and the father explains his sadness and reassures him.

passage: In the village house, the women had gone home after the prayers for Dadi. Farida peeped into the back room. Abba was sitting on the charpai, his face in his hands, crying without sound. Farida froze. Her tummy went tight. She had never seen Abba cry. She backed away quietly and sat by the hens, not talking. After a while Abba came and sat beside her. "You saw me crying?" Farida nodded. "I am sad because I miss Dadi. It is okay to be sad. And I am still here for you." Farida crept into his arms. "Me too, Abba."

qa.q: Where was Abba sitting when Farida saw him cry?
qa.a: He was sitting on the charpai in the back room.

qa.q: How did Farida feel when she saw Abba crying?
qa.a: She felt scared and worried, her tummy tight, because she had never seen him cry.

qa.q: What did Abba do that a wise parent would do?
qa.a: He came to Farida, named his sadness about Dadi, said it was okay to be sad and reassured her he was still there.

qa.q: What would change if Abba had hidden all his grief?
qa.a: Farida might learn that sadness is frightening and should be hidden, and fear her own sad feelings.

grounding: A young girl is scared to see her father crying for Dadi, and he explains his grief and reassures her he is still there.
